title: The poor people's Bible
hook: colored windows told Bible stories to people who couldn't read

segments.voice: Yesterday, beads of prayer, the rosary and the Jesus Prayer on the knotted rope. Your line was counting love. Whose ten good things did you count? Day eight hundred forty-four.

Late afternoon, and a patch of blue and red light is sliding slowly across a stone floor. Follow it up to where it comes from, and there's a window, high in the wall, made of small pieces of colored glass. Look closer, and the colors become people. A man in a boat. A woman at a well. A shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. A whole story, told in light, pane by pane, from the bottom of the window to the top. Today: the poor people's Bible.

Stained glass. The glass gets its color as it's made, and then the details, faces, hands, the folds of a robe, are painted on with dark paint and fired so they hold. Lead strips join the pieces like the lines in a coloring book. In the great churches of the middle ages, windows like these told the Bible's stories, and the lives of the saints, to people who couldn't read. A pope, Gregory the Great, wrote to a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his church. Don't destroy them, Gregory told him. What writing gives to those who can read, a picture gives to those who can't. Some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible. Some historians wonder how much anyone could make out of a window that high. But even from the floor, the light did its work. Windows often paired stories: one from the Old Testament beside one from the New, so that, say, Jonah coming out of the fish sits near Jesus rising from the tomb. Often you read them from the bottom up. There's a line that fits. In the King James Bible, John writes, "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." A stained glass window is dark from the outside. You only see its story from inside, when the sun comes through. Christians have not all loved these windows. In some times and places, reformers broke them, believing images drew worship away from God. Other Protestants kept and made new ones. Churches of different traditions use them still.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at light through colored glass. If you can, find some: a bottle, a glass of juice or wine, a colored jar, a window, even a phone screen turned to a single color. Hold it up to a lamp or the window. Watch the color the light makes. Notice that the glass does nothing on its own; it waits for the light. If you pray, you can give thanks for the light. If you don't, simply watch it. The bell holds the time.
Stained glass. Colored glass, painted and leaded into windows that tell the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.
Your line: light tells stories. Today, notice where the light falls in a room you love, and what it shows you that you'd missed. Day eight hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Stained glass windows still tell Bible stories in churches of different traditions, and churches sometimes hold tours or talks that walk people through a window's story from bottom to top.

fork.setup: you're Gregory the Great. a bishop writes that he has smashed the pictures in his church so no one worships them. what do you tell him?
options: don't destroy them: a picture gives to those who can't read what writing gives to readers.
fork.reveal: Gregory told the bishop not to destroy them: pictures teach those who cannot read.

original.note: Latin: the Bible of the poor, a name later given to picture Bibles and windows like these.

trapdoor: what you thought: pretty church windows.
what it means: windows that told the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.
what a scholar hears: Gregory the Great's letter to Serenus of Marseilles, typological pairing of the Old and New Testaments, and the later iconoclasm of some reformers.

sources.ref: Gregory the Great, Letter to Serenus, Bishop of Marseilles (Registrum 11.10)

notes: Claims rule: no dates or quantities given; 'people who couldn't read' follows the outline hook.
Gregory's letter to Serenus paraphrased; reference number (Registrum 11.10, sometimes 11.13) needs a check.

'Biblia pauperum' properly names a later genre of block-book picture Bibles; the script says 'some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible' and the original note says the name was 'later given to picture Bibles and windows like these'. Confirm fair.
Typological pairing (Jonah / Resurrection) is common in medieval windows; Matthew 12:40 supports the link. Confirm 'often'.
Glass technique (pot-metal color, painted and fired details, lead cames): confirm summary.
Iconoclasm: 'in some times and places, reformers broke them', with other Protestants keeping and making windows; ranks no one. Confirm.
Original is Latin, flagged as Latin in the note.
Editor: hook close fixed (it said 'today's word is the window'; the title is the poor people's Bible); garbled 'the way the light rises' replaced.
Editor 2: 'you read them from the bottom up' softened to 'often' (not true of every window); stock 'Settle, and breathe' cut.
Audit: 'fearing images' was an unfair, dismissive gloss on reformers' iconoclasm; now states their reason (concern that images drew worship from God). John 1:5 KJV checked.
